Daniel’s post leans on an unstated but important conflation: “P=NP” would not make “cracking a hash” *automatically* trivial in the everyday sense, even though it would be devastating to the *theory* that standard hashes rely on. The clean statement is: if \(P=NP\), then NP search problems become solvable in polynomial time, and that strongly suggests the nonexistence of cryptographic one‑way functions (and thus no secure hash functions in the usual sense). But “polynomial time” can still be astronomically large; the difference between “provably efficient” and “practically feasible” matters here, especially because hashes are parameterized by output length and because the polynomial’s degree/constants could be enormous. So the joke lands philosophically, but it also smuggles in a “poly = easy” assumption that complexity theorists are careful to avoid (see the broader cryptography framing in [Goldreich, *Foundations of Cryptography*](https://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~oded/foc.html)).

There’s a second blind spot: using an MD5 hash as a commitment to priority is weaker than the post implies—*even before* any hypothetical \(P=NP\) world. MD5 is collision-broken, meaning an adversary can, in principle, craft two different “sketches” with the same digest; that doesn’t automatically enable a preimage attack on *this* specific hash, but it does undermine the rhetorical function of “I committed to a document” when the hash function itself is no longer a reliable commitment scheme. If the goal is “more distributed,” what actually increases evidentiary weight is not repetition of the same hash, but anchoring: multiple independent timestamps/archives, a modern hash (e.g., SHA‑256), and ideally a signature. The Gödel–Escher–Bach vibe is real, but the more interesting recursion here is that the credibility of the commitment depends on exactly the kind of hardness assumptions that \(P=NP\) would call into question.
